Issued at 225 AM EDT Mon Jul 27 2026

Today through Tonight

An upper level ridge will continue to build eastward within modest 
westerly WAA. This WAA within the lower levels will continue to push 
temperatures and dew points well above normal building deep 
instability across the region. MUCAPE values will exceed 3000 J/kg 
by noon, with values likely pushing above 4000 J/KG towards the 
middle of the afternoon through the evening. Shear will also be 
plentiful as the jet stream remains aloft, with 35-50kt of effective 
shear. The combination of high instability and plentiful bulk shear 
will lead to a potent airmass, but the source of upward motion to 
initiate these thunderstorms is still a bit of an enigma. There is 
building confidence on a convective complex initiating along a weak 
shortwave early this morning over the upper Great Lakes region, with 
a majority of the CAMs pushing this complex southward into the Ohio 
Valley this afternoon. The primary threat with this thunderstorm 
complex will be wind gusts of 60-80MPH, but small hail and an 
isolated tornado cannot be completely ruled out. 

Even with this additional confidence in general timing, specifics on 
timing and location remain fairly uncertain within the previously 
mentioned window due to somewhat ambiguous storm motions. Unlike 
strongly forced events, storm motion will greatly depend on the 
placement of any developing cold pools and its relation to the 
ongoing thermodynamic parameters. This could lead to a storm motion 
range from 340 degrees to potentially 20 degrees over the course of 
this event. Also, CAMs notoriously struggle with translation speed 
and longevity of these thermodynamically induced convective 
complexes due to underestimating cold pool density and interaction 
within the ongoing environment. This is a lot of information to say, 
be very hesitant on taking any CAM reflectivity output verbatim this 
afternoon, and thus confidence in thunderstorm passage for any 
specific location will likely have to wait until 3-6 hours ahead of 
arrival. 

After this first convective threat this afternoon, additional 
thunderstorms are expected to develop along and ahead of a diffuse 
frontal boundary between 01-08Z. As with the first round, confidence 
is fairly low on any specifics, but the overall atmospheric 
parameters will remain potent enough for an additional severe threat 
with wind once again being the primary threat. This time, greatest 
confidence will shift towards NE portions of the area, as this 
portion looks to have slightly greater surface confluence and 
therefor a greater confidence in convective forcing. 

The temperature forecast today will also be fickle and will greatly 
depend on thunderstorm timing and location. The WAA previously 
mentioned will push a very humid airmass into the region with dew 
points likely nearing 80 and temperatures pushing into the low 90s. 
This combination will likely lead to a prolonged period of heat 
index values above 100 and a few hours between 105-110. For this 
reason, a Heat Advisory has been issued. The current ending time for 
the advisory will be 01Z, but this could be canceled early depending 
on cooling impacts from afternoon convection. As stated, a frontal 
passage is expected overnight into tuesday morning. The front is not 
strong, but will still push temperatures back towards seasonal for 
the coming week.

Tuesday through Sunday...

Strengthening hot and humid upper subtropical ridge over western 
North America...will be offset partially by progression of smaller 
weaknesses plunging from north-central CONUS to Ohio Valley...which 
will likely result in slightly below-normal warmth and humidity 
across central Indiana through at least Thursday morning.  First 
cool front progged to push south across the region around dawn 
Tuesday, with northerly gusts actually up to 20-25 mph for many 
locations...only allowing low to mid-80s for central/northern 
counties, and noticeably lower humidity for all by late evening.

Tuesday night to Wednesday night to host most pleasant conditions, 
as weak but amplified surface high pressure builds south from James 
Bay into much of the Midwest...and ridge axis' alignment near the 
Wabash Valley maintaining lower dewpoints and readings for most of 
the region into early Thursday...with highs Wednesday around 80-85F 
amid more September-like breezes...flanked by consecutive overnights 
with lows around 60F.

Late work week to transition warmer and touch more humid as upper 
ridge tries to build east across central US...which will at least 
push the surface high out of the region, returning light southerly
